report:
### Research Conclusion

The claim that capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans is **unproven and speculative**. While laboratory research shows that capsaicin exhibits anti-cancer properties against human breast cancer cells in culture, there is currently a lack of clinical trial evidence establishing capsaicin as an effective cancer treatment in human patients.

### Key Evidence

* **Laboratory (*In Vitro*) Studies:** In vitro experiments demonstrate that capsaicin can inhibit proliferation, reduce cell viability, and induce programmed cell death (apoptosis) in human breast cancer cell lines, such as MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 (https://www.dovepress.com/capsaicin-inhibits-proliferation-and-induces-apoptosis-in-breast-cance-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT).
* **Clinical Human Efficacy:** Medical literature reviews and fact-checks highlight that translating lab findings into human cancer treatments remains speculative (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/). Major hurdles include determining safe, effective dosing and delivering capsaicin directly to tumor sites in humans (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/).
* **Current Clinical Role:** In human trials involving breast cancer patients, capsaicin is studied for supportive management—specifically using high-concentration capsaicin patches to treat post-surgical or chemotherapy-induced neuropathic pain—rather than for treating the tumor itself (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/18/14/2355).
